structural_claim_verifiable_by_reading: Every class-keyed table returns ONE answer per class. So two companies of the same class can differ only where RUN-DERIVED evidence reaches, and for ADVERTISING_PLATFORM even the competitive ladder is class-derived. This is a code fact, not an inference.
not_established: That these companies read alike ON THE PAGE. The four fields that DO differ for the semiconductors are the ladder-derived ones, and those are what a reader sees first in the introduction and the competitive section. The page may differentiate more than 8/12 suggests, or less. Capture the pair in Batch B as evidence beside this number.

NVIDIA Corporation.identity: NVIDIA Corporation is a semiconductor business that runs on design and manufacture of a physical product sold into a capacity-constrained supply chain.
NVIDIA Corporation.economic_role: It competes in a market of few credible suppliers; position turns on process capability and on access to manufacturing capacity; demand reaches it cyclical and inventory-amplified: end demand is smoothed by channel inventory, so orders overshoot in both directions.
NVIDIA Corporation.strategic_position: Its position is contested directly by AI computing processor products and accelerated computing solutions, and customers can substitute rental and used equipment in place of a new purchase.
NVIDIA Corporation.central_question: how much capacity to commit, and when, given that the commitment to manufacturing and foundry cost is made before the unit volume it is meant to serve?
level2_business_model: How the business makes money: design and manufacture of a physical product sold into a capacity-constrained supply chain.
Who the customers are: concentrated — a small number of large buyers can move a quarter on their own ordering decisions.
How it prices: negotiated contract price by product generation, with volume and long-term supply commitments.
What growth does to margin: HIGH and two-sided: fixed manufacturing cost rewards utilisation and punishes an idle line.
What it depends on: few qualified suppliers with long lead times; substitution is slow and expensive.
level4_competition: Keeping the existing fleet running longer
Rental and used equipment in place of a new purchase
what_matters_now: Growth here has to come from unit volume, product and node mix and average selling price — there is no fourth source, so a plan that does not name one of those is not a growth plan.
Move on capacity commitment at a size that can be reversed inside one planning cycle, and instrument it so the result is readable before the next commitment.
competitive_rivals: Keeping the existing fleet running longer

Microsoft Corporation.identity: Microsoft Corporation is a software platform business that runs on recurring software subscription: revenue is contracted and renews, so the installed base carries next period's revenue before any new sale.
Microsoft Corporation.economic_role: It competes in a market of many differentiated vendors competing on capability and switching cost rather than on price alone; demand reaches it budgeted and recurring; new bookings are discretionary, the renewal base is not.
Microsoft Corporation.strategic_position: Its position is contested less by a named firm than by the alternatives its customers already have: customers can substitute automation absorbing the task itself, and customers can internalise the work themselves — the customer's own engineering, and the alternative may be delaying the purchase altogether — renewing nothing and keeping the current process, and the economics that decide the contest are high operating leverage — delivery cost rises far more slowly than contracted revenue, so incremental revenue is unusually valuable.
Microsoft Corporation.central_question: what to charge, and for what, without losing more customer count than the price gains?
level2_business_model: How the business makes money: recurring software subscription: revenue is contracted and renews, so the installed base carries next period's revenue before any new sale.
Who the customers are: many accounts of uneven size; concentration risk sits in the largest contracts, not in the count.
How it prices: list price with negotiated discount, per seat or per unit of usage.
What growth does to margin: delivery cost rises far more slowly than contracted revenue, so incremental revenue is unusually valuable.
What it depends on: compute and bandwidth from a small number of providers.
level4_competition: Renewing nothing and keeping the current process
metrics: contracted backlog or remaining performance obligations
what_matters_now: Growth here has to come from customer count, seats or usage per customer and list and realised price — there is no fourth source, so a plan that does not name one of those is not a growth plan.

Alphabet Inc..identity: Alphabet Inc. is a software platform business that runs on attention resold to advertisers: revenue is an auction price per impression, so nothing is contracted forward and each period's revenue has to be re-earned by engagement.
Alphabet Inc..economic_role: It competes in a market of a few platforms holding most of the inventory, competing for advertiser budget against every other channel that can prove return; demand reaches it discretionary and cyclical: advertising budget is among the first spending cut in a downturn and among the first restored.
Alphabet Inc..strategic_position: Its position is contested less by a named firm than by the alternatives its customers already have: customers can substitute another surface holding the same attention hour and automation absorbing the task itself, and customers can internalise the work themselves — the advertiser spending the budget on its own channels, and the economics that decide the contest are high operating leverage — serving one more impression costs almost nothing, so incremental revenue is unusually valuable — and the same fixed base makes an engagement decline expensive quickly.
Alphabet Inc..central_question: What does the published record establish about Alphabet Inc., and what would have to be true before a commitment rests on it?
level2_business_model: How the business makes money: attention resold to advertisers: revenue is an auction price per impression, so nothing is contracted forward and each period's revenue has to be re-earned by engagement.
Who the customers are: two-sided and asymmetric — many small advertisers with a long tail, and a user base that pays nothing and can leave freely.
How it prices: real-time auction per impression, so price is set by competing advertisers rather than by the platform.
What growth does to margin: serving one more impression costs almost nothing, so incremental revenue is unusually valuable — and the same fixed base makes an engagement decline expensive quickly.
What it depends on: the distribution channel is the binding supplier: the operating systems, browsers and devices that decide what can be measured.
